'''Virginia Tower Norwood''' (January 8, 1927 – March 26, 2023) was an American aerospace engineer, inventor, and physicist.<ref name="LandsatAward">{{cite web |title=Virginia T. Norwood, Engineer Responsible for First Landsat Multispectral Scanner, Receives 2021 ASPRS Lifetime Achievement Award |url=https://landsat.gsfc.nasa.gov/article/virginia-t-norwood-engineer-responsible-first-landsat-multispectral-scanner-receives-2021 |publisher=Landsat Science |access-date=June 30, 2021 |archive-date=June 23, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210623020722/https://landsat.gsfc.nasa.gov/article/virginia-t-norwood-engineer-responsible-first-landsat-multispectral-scanner-receives-2021 |url-status=dead }}</ref> She was best known for her contribution to the [[Landsat program]],<ref name="TechReview">{{cite web|last1=Dragoon|first1=Alice|date=June 29, 2021|title=The woman who brought us the world|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2021/06/29/1025732/the-woman-who-brought-us-the-world/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210704075023/https://www.technologyreview.com/2021/06/29/1025732/the-woman-who-brought-us-the-world/|archive-date=July 4, 2021|access-date=June 30, 2021|publisher=MIT Technology Review}}</ref> having designed the [[Multispectral Scanner]]<ref name="Landsat">{{cite web |last1=Rocchio |first1=Laura |title=Virginia T. Norwood: The Mother of Landsat |url=https://landsat.gsfc.nasa.gov/article/virginia-t-norwood-mother-landsat |publisher=Landsat Science |access-date=June 30, 2021 |date=August 7, 2020}}</ref><ref name="Pennisi">{{cite journal |last1=Pennisi |first1=Elizabeth |author-link=Elizabeth Pennisi |title=Meet the Landsat pioneer who fought to revolutionize Earth observation |journal=Science |date=September 10, 2021 |volume=373 |issue=6561 |page=1292 |doi=10.1126/science.acx9080|s2cid=239215521 }}</ref> which was first used on [[Landsat 1]]. She has been called "The Mother of Landsat" for this work.<ref name="NPR-Obit">{{cite web |last1=Radde |first1=Kaitlyn |title=Virginia Norwood, a pioneer in satellite land imaging, dies at age 96 |url=https://www.npr.org/2023/03/31/1167375710/virginia-norwood-satellite-land-imaging-nasa-died |publisher=[[NPR]] |access-date=April 2, 2023 |date=March 31, 2023 |quote=When asked if she liked the nickname ''Mother of Landsat'', she told NASA: 'Yes. I like it, and it's apt. I created it; I birthed it; and I fought for it.'}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Virginia Tower was born on January 8, 1927, at [[Fort Totten (Queens)|Fort Totten]] in New York City, United States<ref name=":1" /> the eldest daughter of Eleanor Monroe and John Vogler Tower.<ref name = McClain>{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/12/science/space/virginia-norwood-dead.html|title = Virginia Norwood, 'Mother' of Satellite Imaging Systems, Dies at 96|last = McClain|first = Dylan Loeb|date = April 12, 2023|accessdate = April 12, 2023|newspaper = [[The New York Times]]|url-access = limited}}</ref> He was an Army officer, had a master's degree in physics, and later taught at [[Carnegie Mellon University|Carnegie Tech]]. Her mother was skilled in mathematics and languages and studied independently.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |first1=Brian |last1=Murphy |date=March 30, 2023 |title=Virginia Norwood, pioneered Earth imagery as 'mother of Landsat,' dies at 96 |language=en-US |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2023/03/30/virginia-norwood-landsat-engineer-dies/ |access-date=March 31, 2023 |issn=0190-8286|url-access = limited}}</ref> Her father actively encouraged young Virginia's interest in physics and mathematics; he gave her a slide rule when she was nine years old, and helped to develop her mathematical skills.<ref name = McClain/><ref>{{Cite web |date=August 7, 2020 |title=Virginia T. Norwood: The Mother of Landsat {{!}} Landsat Science |url=https://landsat.gsfc.nasa.gov/article/virginia-t-norwood-the-mother-of-landsat/ |access-date=March 29, 2023 |publisher=landsat.gsfc.nasa.gov |language=en-US}}</ref> The family moved around with her father's military career, living in Panama, Oklahoma, and Bermuda.<ref name = McClain/> Once military families were sent back to the American mainland following the [[attack on Pearl Harbor]] in December 1941, she was a pupil at five high schools. In 1943, her guidance counselor in high school suggested she become a librarian due to her intelligence, but she was much more interested in numbers than words.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=The woman who brought us the world |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2021/06/29/1025732/the-woman-who-brought-us-the-world/ |access-date=March 31, 2023 |publisher=MIT Technology Review |language=en}}</ref>

Norwood was accepted into the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] with a partial scholarship in 1944.<ref name="Landsat" /> She graduated in 1947 with a degree in mathematical physics.<ref name="Landsat" />

While working at the [[Signal Corps (United States Army)|United States Army Signal Corps]] in [[New Jersey]], she took engineering classes through a [[Rutgers University]] extension programme.<ref name=Landsat/>

== Career ==
A year after graduation from MIT she was hired by the [[Signal Corps (United States Army)|U.S. Army Signal Corps]] Laboratories in [[Fort Monmouth]], [[New Jersey]]. She began working on weather radar. While there, she designed a radar reflector for weather balloons before progressing to work on microwave antenna design.<ref name=Landsat/>

After five years at the Signal Corps she moved to [[Los Angeles]] and began working for [[Hughes Aircraft Company]]. She worked there for 36 years on a range of projects that included antenna design, communications links, optics, and the Landsat scanners.<ref name=Landsat/> During that period she designed the microwave transmitter that [[Surveyor 1]] used to transmit data and images back to earth.<ref name=TechReview/>

Norwood designed a six-band multispectral scanner for use on the first Landsat mission. Due to mission constraints the prototype was revised to use only four bands.<ref name=Landsat/> The [[Multispectral Scanner]], as it was known, was carried on [[Landsat 1]]. An improved seven band version, known as the [[Thematic Mapper]] was later included on [[Landsat 4]].<ref name="LandsatMSS">{{cite web |title=The Multispectral Scanner System |url=https://landsat.gsfc.nasa.gov/multispectral-scanner-system |publisher=Landsat Science |access-date=June 30, 2021}}</ref>

Norwood retired in 1989.<ref name=TechReview/> A biographical article published by [[NASA]] in 2020 referred to her as "The Mother of Landsat".<ref name="Landsat" />

=== Patents ===
Norwood filed and held three patents. Two of them are a radar reflector designed to track weather balloons and a novel folded tracking antenna.

== Awards ==
In 1979, Norwood received the William T. Pecora Award.<ref name="Pecora Recipients">{{cite web |title=William T. Pecora List of Recipients |url=https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/national-land-imaging-program/william-t-pecora-list-recipientsl |publisher=USGS |access-date=July 5, 2021}}</ref> The award recognizes achievements in the scientific and technical remote sensing community, as well as contributions leading to successful practical applications of remote sensing. The award is sponsored jointly by the U.S. Department of the Interior and the [[NASA|National Aeronautics and Space Administration]].<ref name="Pecora">{{cite web |title=William T. Pecora Award |url=https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/national-land-imaging-program/william-t-pecora-award-0l |publisher=USGS |access-date=July 5, 2021}}</ref>

In 2021, Norwood was given an Honorary Lifetime Achievement Award <ref name="ASPRS">{{cite web |title=2021 Award Winners |url=https://www.asprs.org/awards-and-scholarships/award-winners/2021-award-winners.html |publisher=ASPRS |access-date=June 30, 2021}}</ref><ref name="LandsatAward" /> by the [[American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing]], the highest honour that society bestows on any individual.<ref name="ASPRSHonour">{{cite web |title=Honorary Lifetime Achievement Award |url=https://www.asprs.org/awards-and-scholarships/honorary-member-award.html |publisher=ASPRS |access-date=June 30, 2021}}</ref>

Norwood was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in February 2023<ref>{{cite web |title=National Academy of Engineering Elects 106 Members and 18 International Members |url=https://www.nae.edu/289843/NAENewClass2023 |publisher=[[National Academy of Engineering]] |access-date=April 2, 2023 |language=en |date=February 7, 2023 |quote='''Norwood, Virginia''', manager (retired), Earth Resources Requirements NASA Systems Division, Hughes Aircraft Co., Topanga, Calif. For the original design and implementation of radar multispectral satellite systems forming the basis for Earth-observing Landsat missions.}}</ref> and in 2025 posthumously inducted into the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{cite web |title=NIHF Virginia Norwood Multispectral Scanner |url=https://www.invent.org/inductees/virginia-norwood |website=www.invent.org |publisher=National Inventors Hall of Fame |access-date=1 April 2025 |date=2025}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Virginia Tower married Lawrence Russell Norwood, her third-semester calculus instructor and the president of the MIT mathematics club. They married on the day after she completed her bachelor's degree in mathematics.<ref name = McClain/> They had three children before divorcing. She went on to marry Maurice Schaeffer.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" />

Norwood died at her home in [[Topanga, California]], on March 26, 2023, at age 96.<ref name=":1"/><ref>{{Cite web |date=March 29, 2023 |title=Bidding Farewell to Virginia T. Norwood, the Mother of Landsat {{!}} Landsat Science |url=https://landsat.gsfc.nasa.gov/article/bidding-farewell-to-virginia-t-norwood-the-mother-of-landsat/ |access-date=March 29, 2023 |publisher=landsat.gsfc.nasa.gov |language=en-US}}</ref>
